un-ga-res-32:
Early in 1946 the UN General Assembly took up the case of Spain, then ruled by General Franco. Resolution 32 recalls two wartime pledges. At San Francisco, states set up with Axis help were barred. At Potsdam, the big three powers vowed not to back Spain's entry to the UN. The Assembly backs both pledges in full.

Members are urged to act in the letter and spirit of those pledges in all future dealings with Spain. The text stops short of a break in ties. But it marks Franco's Spain as a state born of fascist aid. As such, it is unfit for a UN seat while his regime lasts.
un-ga-res-a-69-32:
An arms race in outer space must be stopped before it starts, says Resolution A/69/32, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The text recalls the shared gain of all mankind in the study and use of space for peaceful ends. It voices grave concern at the chance of weapons spreading to orbit, and recalls the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which bars mass-kill arms from space.

The rules now in force, the Assembly holds, do not by themselves bar a space arms race. The legal frame must be made stronger and more firm. A draft treaty on the point, laid before the Conference on Disarmament, is welcomed as a step in that work.
un-sc-res-32: Fighting on the island of Java drew the Security Council back in Resolution 32, passed on 26 August 1947. Armed work by Dutch forces on the soil of the Republic of Indonesia still ran on. The vote calls both the Netherlands and the Republic back to the Council's call of 1 August 1947. That call had ordered a cease-fire and a peaceful fix to their fight. Both sides are told to hew to it in strict form.
un-sc-res-232: Dated 1960 in the catalog, Resolution 232 records formal action by the United Nations Security Council. The Council's fifteen members vote on draft texts, and adopted ones enter the record as numbered resolutions. The library holds the complete text in the form transcribed for English Wikisource from the official UN record. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-1332: Readers meet Resolution 1332 here as a Security Council record, catalogued with a date of 2000. un-sc-res-1532:

The freeze reaches Taylor, his family, and close associates, and it covers funds held in other countries. States must stop those people from moving or spending the money, with narrow limits for basic needs. The text is a clear case of the Council using money as a tool to guard a peace deal.
un-sc-res-1632: From 2005, Resolution 1632 records a decision of the fifteen-member Security Council in official wording. The source is English Wikisource's transcription of the UN record. un-sc-res-1732: From 2006, Resolution 1732 records a formal decision of the Security Council, preserved in official-record form. The transcription here is English Wikisource's. Inside, the members build their case in the preamble before acting in the operative part, a rhythm as regular as a court's. The whole performance is kept, so the reasoning survives with the result.
un-sc-res-1932: Kept under number 1932, a Security Council resolution survives in official-record form through English Wikisource. plos-pone-0000032:
Marina Bacac, Paolo Provero, Nathalie Mayran, and co-authors found a survival signal hiding around tumors in a 2006 study. The stroma is the supporting tissue that surrounds a tumor, and it responds when cancer invades. The team measured that stromal response in mice as tumors spread into it.

A gene pattern in the responding stroma predicted how long prostate and breast cancer patients survived. In other words, tissue that is not itself cancer still carries a forecast of the patient's fate. Doctors usually grade the tumor alone; this work argues the neighborhood matters too. Such signatures could one day help decide which patients need aggressive treatment and which can safely be spared it.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d32: Alexander Kirk, the American ambassador in Egypt, wrote to the Secretary of State on September 10, 1943, and his dispatch is Document 32 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The record names no topic for this dispatch.

frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d232:
The United States Chiefs of Staff issued paper C.C.S. 390/1 aboard the Iowa on 18 November 1943, on future operations in the Southeast Asia Command. It answers a paper from the British side and guards the Combined Chiefs of Staff's right to decide more than grand strategy alone.

The American chiefs hold that the combined body should choose among courses of action, and fix their order and timing, for Southeast Asia. Since the United States cannot supply what Operation First Culverin would need, they agree that Operation Buccaneer should be mounted as early as possible. They also ask the Southeast Asia commander to study further land, sea, and air moves to pin down Japanese forces in south Burma.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d332: President Roosevelt sent Ambassador Alexander Kirk a one-line memorandum at Cairo on 26 November 1943. It asks Kirk to have Wadsworth, the American consul general at Beirut, come down to Cairo when Roosevelt returns there, which he expects to be about Thursday or Friday. frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d432: Harry Hopkins sent Ambassador Steinhardt an urgent telegram from Cairo on 3 December 1943 about the greeting party for President Inönü of Turkey. Major John Boettiger is accompanying the President's plane to Adana that day, to extend Roosevelt's greetings to Inönü on his arrival and to travel back with him. Randolph Churchill is flying on a similar mission in the Prime Minister's plane. Hopkins adds a small point of ceremony and tactics in one line: the President would be pleased to have Inönü ride in the American plane.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d532:
Ambassador Laurence Steinhardt in Ankara wrote on December 24, 1943 to Paul H. Alling, chief of the State Department's Division of Near Eastern Affairs. Writing to a division chief meant writing to the desk that ran Turkish policy day by day. The State Department printed the letter in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Steinhardt's channel to Alling was where embassy reporting met Washington policymaking on Turkey and the Near East. Three weeks after the Cairo meeting with President İnönü, the Turkish question remained open and delicate. For readers, the letter shows diplomacy at the working level: an ambassador and a desk chief keeping a difficult account in order.
frus-1944-quebec-d32:
A second message from Harry Hopkins to Prime Minister Churchill is dated August 28, 1944. The State Department printed it in the Quebec 1944 volume, next to its companions of the same date.

Hopkins divided his business among separate messages, a habit he shared with Churchill. His late-August letters to London prepared the Quebec meeting from the American side: who would come, what would be discussed, and what the President hoped to settle. For readers, this message is one panel of a day's concentrated staff work, valuable because it shows how much of a summit happens before the leaders arrive.
frus-1944-quebec-d132:

It is addressed to Roosevelt and Hull, and it concerns Italy rather than the Vatican. Taylor wanted the president briefed by a man on the ground before the reported conference with Churchill.

Taylor urged a frank talk with General William O'Dwyer, who ran the economic section of the Allied Control Commission for Italy. O'Dwyer could explain Italy's relief needs and the plans to meet them, Taylor said. He asked that Hull or Leo Crowley telegraph O'Dwyer at once, ordering him to Washington for consultation without delay.

At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
plos-pbio-0020132:
Philipp Khaitovich, Gunter Weiss, Michael Lachmann, and their group proposed a neutral model of transcriptome change in PLOS Biology in 2004. The transcriptome is the full set of gene messages a tissue makes. The authors ask how much of its change over evolution is driven by selection, and how much is mere drift.

A neutral model gives the null case: change with no selection at all. Only data that beat that baseline need a stronger story. The team found much of the pattern fits drift well. That does not make selection rare, but it sets the bar for claiming it. The paper is a useful guard against over-reading gene data from any two species.
plos-pbio-0020332:
Shelly Beer, Anders Zetterberg, Rebecca A. Ihrie, and their team tested a cancer gene's timing in PLOS Biology in 2004. MYC is a powerful growth gene that can drive tumors when stuck on. The team switched it on in different tissues and at different stages of growth in mice.

The same gene took very different times to cause tumors depending on context. Some settings resisted for long spans, while others fell fast. That gap, called latency, shows cancer is not just about which gene breaks. The state of the cell counts as much. Results like this help explain why one mutation can be deadly in one organ and quiet in another.
plos-pbio-0020432:
Christiane E. Wobus, Stephanie M. Karst, Larissa B. Thackray, and their team grew norovirus in the lab in PLOS Biology in 2004. Noroviruses cause most cases of viral stomach flu, yet they long refused to grow in cell culture, which stalled research. The team's mouse norovirus system broke that barrier.

Grown in culture, the virus favored immune cells: dendritic cells and macrophages. That tropism, its taste for certain cells, shapes how infection starts in the gut. A working culture system lets labs test antivirals and study the virus life cycle at last. The mouse virus now serves as the stand-in for its human kin, which still resist culture.
plos-pone-0000132:
Ximena J. Nelson and Robert R. Jackson published this ecology study in PLOS ONE in 2006. It features a predator from East Africa that, as the title says, chooses malaria vectors as its preferred prey. Malaria vectors are the mosquitoes that carry the malaria parasite to people.

A predator that hunts those mosquitoes by choice is a natural ally in malaria control. The authors document this preference and what it means for the food web around it. The work drew attention because most predators eat mosquitoes only by chance; a specialist hunter raises the prospect of biological control of a deadly disease.
plos-pone-0000232:
Nooshin Tabatabaei-Zavareh, Anastasia Vlasova, Chelsea Pamela Greenwood, and colleagues published this stem cell paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Natural killer cells are frontline immune defenders, and making them in the lab from embryonic stem cells could supply therapies. The authors characterize the developmental pathway those cells follow as they grow from stem cells in vitro.

Knowing each step of natural killer cell development lets researchers steer and check the process. The paper maps that path in the dish. It supports efforts to grow immune cells on demand, a goal for cancer therapy where a patient's own cells are in short supply.
plos-pone-0000332:
Erik Cobo, Albert Selva-O'Callagham, Josep-Maria Ribera, and colleagues published this randomized trial in PLOS ONE in 2007. It asks whether statistical reviewers improve reporting in biomedical articles. Manuscripts were randomly assigned review with or without a statistician's input, and the quality of reporting was compared.

Poor statistical reporting wastes research and misleads doctors. The trial gives rare experimental evidence on an editorial practice usually adopted on faith. Its result speaks to journal editors deciding whether statistical review is worth its cost and delay. Good reporting is not a small thing: doctors act on what papers say. Weak numbers can mislead care, so proof of what helps is worth having.
plos-pone-0000432:
Jonas Dahlberg and colleagues linked a common gene variant to salt handling in the body, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The gene is NEDD4L, which helps control sodium channels in the kidney. The team tested whether a polymorphism in it goes with increased salt sensitivity. They also checked two hormone-related markers, P-renin and Nt-proANP, which moved in opposite directions.

Salt sensitivity, where blood pressure rises sharply with dietary salt, varies from person to person and runs in families. A gene that explains part of that spread could help identify who most needs to cut salt. The study connects a kidney sodium channel regulator to everyday cardiovascular risk.
plos-pone-0000532:
Andrés Muñoz-Alarcón and colleagues compared fly and human versions of a disease of the cell's scaffolding, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Lamins are proteins that line the nucleus and give it structure. Human mutations in them cause laminopathies. That family of disorders affects muscle, fat, and aging. The team characterized lamin mutation phenotypes in Drosophila and compared them to the human diseases.

A fly that shows the same cellular defects as a human patient becomes a fast, cheap model for testing treatments. Comparing phenotypes across species also shows which parts of lamin function are ancient. The study validates the fly as a stand-in for a group of rare but revealing human disorders.
plos-pone-0000632:
Hassan Khan, Ather M. Taqui, Muhammad Rizwanulhaq Khawaja and colleagues compared two ways of teaching medical students, in PLOS ONE in 2007. One group learned by problem-based learning, working through cases. The other followed a conventional lecture-based curriculum. The subject under test was health research: what students knew about it and how they felt about doing it.

The authors argue that medical curricula in developing countries should stress research training. Students who can judge and do research strengthen a whole health system. By comparing knowledge and attitudes side by side, the study gives curriculum planners direct evidence about which approach builds research-minded doctors.
plos-pone-0000732:
Wei Hou, John Stephen F. Yap, Song Wu and colleagues tackled the fine-mapping of trait genes in breeding experiments, for PLOS ONE in 2007. Mapping quantitative trait loci, or QTL, aims ultimately at cloning the actual genes behind farm and medical traits. Yet only a small portion, at most about one percent of detected QTL, had been characterized at the molecular level.

Their method haplotypes a quantitative trait using a high-density map in experimental crosses. Haplotyping reads the pattern of inherited blocks, not single markers. Denser, smarter mapping could raise that one-percent success rate. Breeders and medical geneticists share the same bottleneck, so a better method serves both fields.
plos-pone-0000832:
Harald Staiger, Fausto Machicao, Norbert Stefan and co-authors tied new diabetes risk genes to how well the pancreas makes insulin. Type 2 diabetes sets in when the body resists insulin and the beta cells that make it wear out. Diet, low activity, and a web of inherited traits all play a part. Genome scans had just found new risk spots, but not what they do.

The team's title states the link: variants in those new risk spots set beta-cell function. In other words, the risk acts through the insulin-making cells themselves, not just through insulin resistance. Knowing where each risk gene does its harm tells drug makers where to aim. The study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2007.
plos-pone-0000932:
Raquel Ferreira, Claudio Lazzari, Marcelo Lorenzo and colleagues asked how blood sucking bugs find veins under the skin, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Some of these insects slide their mouthparts straight into a vessel and feed from inside it. How they locate the vessel was largely unknown, and less than five percent of skin holds vessels at all.

The team tested whether the bugs read skin surface temperature as a guide. Warm patches could betray the blood flowing below. Knowing how a blood feeder aims matters beyond curiosity. These bugs spread serious diseases, and each step in feeding is a possible place to block them.
plos-pone-0001032:
Jae Hyang Lim, Hirofumi Jono, Tomoaki Koga and colleagues studied a protein that brakes inflammation from a common airway germ, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Non-typeable Haemophilus influenzae causes respiratory infections in adults and children. The inflammation it triggers runs largely through NF-kappaB, a master switch for immune genes.

The tumor suppressor CYLD acts as a negative regulator of that switch. The team examined its role in middle ear and lung inflammation in mice infected with the germ. A natural brake, understood well, suggests how harmful inflammation might be eased without silencing defense. Ear infections in children are a major target.
plos-pone-0001132:
White blood cells must crawl out of the bloodstream and into tissue to fight infection. Jürgen Schymeinsky and co-authors traced one step of that journey in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They focused on Syk, a signaling protein found mainly in blood cells, and on a second protein, PI3K-delta.

The authors show that Syk controls the movement of PI3K-delta to the leading edge of a migrating white blood cell. That placement helps the cell build a lamellipodium, the flat front extension it uses to move. The pathway they map connects the cell's grip on blood vessel walls to its crawling machinery.
plos-pone-0001232:
Glycans, the sugar chains decorating proteins, are built step by step by many enzymes, and finding which gene makes which enzyme is slow work. Harumi Yamamoto and colleagues present a screening method in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They call it CIRES, for correlation index-based responsible-enzyme gene screening, and it uses DNA microarray data.

The logic is that an enzyme gene's activity should track the appearance of the glycan it builds. By correlating expression patterns, the method nominates candidate genes for a given step in glycan biosynthesis. Faster gene hunting matters for understanding diseases of abnormal glycosylation.
plos-pone-0001332:
Common painkillers, the NSAIDs, work mainly by blocking cyclooxygenase enzymes, but they have other targets too. Asher Peretz and colleagues explored one such target in new diphenylamine compounds, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Two NSAIDs, diclofenac and meclofenamate, had recently been shown to also affect potassium channels called M-channels.

The authors describe derivatives in which the function switches: cyclooxygenase inhibition fades and M-channel modulation takes over. M-channels calm neuronal excitability, so such compounds interest researchers in pain and epilepsy. The study is medicinal chemistry: reshaping a known drug scaffold toward a new target.
plos-pone-0001532:
Robyn Kim, Aaron Seitz, and Ladan Shams wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on learning with more than one sense. Most learning studies use sight or sound alone. Yet the senses work as a team in daily life, even at early steps. The team tested whether matched sight and sound cues help visual learning more than mixed ones.

Matched cues did boost how well people learned the visual task. The gain shows the senses aid each other when their signals agree. Training that pairs senses with care could speed skill gains. The result also shapes models of how the brain merges sense data.
plos-pone-0001632:
Martine Muleris, Alexandra Chalastanis, Nicolas Meyer, and their co-authors studied unstable chromosomes in bowel cancer for a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. In many tumors, cells gain or lose whole chromosomes or swap pieces of them, a fault called chromosomal instability. It can arise when normal chromosomes are sorted wrongly at cell division, or when chromosome structure is rearranged.

The team focused on tumors that stay near the normal chromosome number, called near-diploid colorectal cancers. They asked which chromosomes each kind of fault tends to hit. The full text gives the chromosome counts and structural changes they found, and the link they report between number changes and structure changes. Knowing which faults come first may help explain how these cancers grow and change.
plos-pone-0001732:
Thilan Wickramarachchi, Yengkhom S. Devi, Asif Mohmmed, and their co-authors identified a new malaria parasite protein in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Plasmodium falciparum causes the deadliest malaria. Its merozoite stage invades red blood cells, and proteins on the merozoite surface or released from its apical organelles are leading vaccine candidates.

The team characterized a novel merozoite apical protein, PfAARP, rich in the amino acid asparagine, and tied it to red cell binding and invasion. The full text gives the gene, the protein's location, and the binding tests. Each new invasion protein is a possible vaccine piece, since blocking invasion stops the parasite's blood stage, the phase that makes people sick.
plos-pone-0001832:
Elisabeth Fonteneau and Heather K. J. van der Lely measured brain responses in language-impaired children in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Specific language impairment, or SLI, affects over 7 percent of children. It is studied as a window onto the biological foundations of language and its evolutionary origins.

Recording electrical brain responses to language stimuli, the team found grammar-specific deficits in the children with SLI. The full text gives the response patterns for grammar versus other language features. A deficit confined to grammar supports the idea that grammar rests on its own brain machinery. That machinery is separate from general intelligence or vocabulary, which shapes how these children should be taught.
plos-pone-0001932:
Pekka Kaitaniemi wrote a theory study in PLOS ONE in 2008 on a neglected number in a common growth law. Allometric equations link a trait to body size with the form Y equals b times X to the power a. They are used across biology, from trees to animals, to scale one measure against another.

Most work focuses on the power a, while the constant b is treated as a mere scaling fix with no meaning. Kaitaniemi shows how real biological facts can be read out of b itself. If he is right, old data sets hold untapped facts, since b has been reported for decades and largely ignored.
plos-pone-0002032:
Matthias Habjan and co-authors showed how some viruses trim their genomes to hide from immunity, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Fast interferon release is the core of innate defense against viruses. Two sensors, RIG-I and MDA5, detect viral RNA by traits such as triple-phosphate ends or double strands, and set off that alarm.

Negative-strand RNA viruses carry genomes whose ends can bear those alarm traits. As the title states, processing the genome's five-prime ends is a strategy these viruses use to avoid RIG-I and the interferon call. Naming the dodge helps design viruses and vaccines that cannot hide.
plos-pone-0002132:
Roger Bate and co-authors bought malaria drugs from pharmacies across Africa and tested what was in them, for a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The team worked in the major cities of six African countries, in the part of the world where malaria hits hardest. They collected a range of antimalarial drugs from private drug shops in city and near-city areas.

Using thin-layer chromatography, a simple lab test that separates the parts of a mixture, they checked drug quality. Fake or weak malaria drugs cost lives, since patients trust pills that may hold too little of the active drug. The study gives hard data on a trade that thrives where checks are rare.
plos-pone-0002232:
Melissa Andrew, Arnold Mitnitski, and Kenneth Rockwood measured how social weakness relates to frailty and death in older people, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Social vulnerability covers things like living alone, low contact with others, and poor support. It is tied to the health of elderly people, but how to measure it, and how it relates to physical frailty, was disputed.

The authors built a social vulnerability index by counting deficits, the same approach used for frailty indexes. They then compared the two measures and their links to mortality. The study gives geriatric care a firmer way to count social risk alongside bodily risk.
plos-pone-0002332:
Selene Báez and Scott Collins tracked what happens when shrubs invade a desert grassland in New Mexico, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Climate change is shifting species ranges worldwide. As invading species enter a community, they alter who interacts with whom, which can reduce the stability that guards biodiversity. Arid lands are seeing this change fast.

In the northern Chihuahuan Desert, the team found shrub invasion decreases plant diversity and alters community stability. Fewer species and a shakier community make the ecosystem less able to absorb drought and other shocks. Their long look at one desert site gives measured weight to a pattern reported across dry regions.
plos-pone-0002432:
Research by Rao and co-authors came out in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Srinivas Rao, Wing-Pui Kong, Chih-Jen Wei, and others. Its subject is multivalent HA DNA Vaccination Protects against Highly Pathogenic H5N1 Avian Influenza Infection in Chickens and Mice. Sustained outbreaks of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5N1 in avian species increase the risk of reassortment and adaptation to humans.

Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside.
plos-pone-0002532:
Hsiao and colleagues set out their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The author list runs from Edward C. Hsiao, Yuko Yoshinaga, Trieu D. Nguyen, and others. Its subject is marking Embryonic Stem Cells with a 2A Self-Cleaving Peptide: A NKX2-5 Emerald GFP BAC Reporter. Fluorescent reporters are useful for assaying gene expression in living cells and for identifying and isolating pure cell populations from heterogeneous cultures.

What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002632:
Work by David Cohen and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was are child and adolescent responses to placebo higher in major depression than in anxiety disorders? a systematic review of Placebo-Controlled trials. The catalog record names David Cohen first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. In a previous report. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002732:
Work by Margarida Cunha-Rodrigues and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was Genistein-Supplemented diet decreases malaria liver infection in mice and constitutes a potential prophylactic strategy. Authorship is credited in the record to Margarida Cunha-Rodrigues and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. In tropical regions millions of people still live at risk of malaria infection. The authors add a further point. Indeed the emergence of resistance to chloroquine and other drugs in use in these areas reinforces the need to implement alternative prophylactic strategies. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start. The full text can be read in the library, and this summary adds nothing beyond the record and abstract held for the entry.
plos-pone-0002832:
Work by Elina Mäntylä and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was from plants to birds: higher avian predation rates in trees responding to insect herbivory. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Elina Mäntylä, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. An understanding of the evolution of potential signals from plants to the predators of their herbivores may provide exciting examples of co-evolution among multiple. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002932:
Matt Finer, Clinton Jenkins, Stuart Pimm and co-authors mapped oil and gas threats in the western Amazon in 2008. That region is the richest part of the Amazon basin for wildlife and home to many indigenous groups. Some of the world's last uncontacted peoples live there in voluntary isolation.

Unlike the eastern Brazilian Amazon, the west was still largely intact at the time. The PLOS ONE paper sets out where energy projects press on wilderness, biodiversity, and indigenous peoples. Conservation planners get a region-wide picture of risk at a moment when choices could still protect large areas.
plos-pone-0003032:
Lorenzo Moroni, Doreen Hamann, Luca Paoluzzi and co-authors built scaffolds for joint tissue repair in 2008. Scaffolds for osteochondral engineering, covering bone plus cartilage, must be mechanically stable. They must also signal cells to regrow both tissues and offer a fully connected pore network for cell movement and growth.

Their approach converges technologies, combining polymer and ceramic composites toward that end, as the title phrases it. Published in PLOS ONE, regenerating articular tissue matters for joint injury and arthritis, where cartilage heals poorly on its own. Scaffold design is a main bottleneck. Full methods, data, and references appear in the complete article for readers who want more detail.
plos-pone-0003132:
Antonio G. Pacheco, Betina Durovni, Solange C. Cavalcante and colleagues study AIDS and tuberculosis together in Rio de Janeiro in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Brazil has offered free combined antiretroviral therapy to all since 1997, which sets the scene for the study. The team used past surveillance records at the population level.

They tracked how often tuberculosis, AIDS, AIDS deaths and combined AIDS-TB infection occurred in the city. Readers get a population view of two linked epidemics under free HIV treatment. The work helps judge where TB control in people with HIV still falls short.
plos-pone-0003232:
Yuki Sugiura, Shuichi Shimma, Yoshiyuki Konishi and colleagues apply imaging mass spectrometry to brain fats in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Gangliosides are particularly abundant in the central nervous system and are thought to play important roles in memory formation, nerve growth, synaptic transmission and other neural functions. Although several molecular species of gangliosides had been characterized, their exact distribution was less clear.

The authors visualize age-dependent accumulation of C20-ganglioside species in the mouse hippocampus, a memory region. Readers see chemistry mapped in place and across age. Spatial maps like this can link specific molecules to the brain regions they may affect.
plos-pone-0003332:
Carolina Rezával, Jimena Berni, Ezequiel Axel Gorostiza and colleagues screen for degeneration genes in flies in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Drosophila is a proven model to study the molecular basis of neurodegenerative diseases. The team carried out a misexpression screen to find genes involved in neurodegeneration. They examined locomotor behaviour in young and aged flies. They thought a progressive loss of function would appear with age.

Their screen uncovers a role for the gene Enabled in progressive neurodegeneration. Readers get a gene lead found by behaviour first, then biology. Fly screens remain a fast way to name genes for study in human brain disease.
plos-pone-0007432: Two patches can share the same brightness meter reading yet look different to us — perception follows edges and structure, not just raw light. The researchers used a technique that reveals which image features drive our judgments of brightness. The results challenge the old idea that brightness comes only from border analysis, showing richer visual clues at work.
plos-pone-0007532: The sleeping-sickness parasite Trypanosoma brucei hides from the immune system under a coat of variant surface glycoprotein. This study blocked production of that coat and found the parasite's whole protein-making machinery ground to a halt. The coat turns out to be so essential that the cell refuses to build anything without it.
plos-pone-0007632: Gene-activity tests for thyroid cancer have been weak partly because they lump too many lesion types together. This study analyzed more classes of thyroid lesions at once and found the diagnostic markers improved. Finer categories make for sharper tests.
plos-pone-0007732: Legionella, the bacterium behind Legionnaires' disease, resists many drugs and invades lung cells. This study shows its TolC protein pumps out antibiotics and helps the early steps of invasion. One protein thus serves both defense and attack — a double target for new drugs.
plos-pone-0007832: Diabetic breathing muscles got a gene readout. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by van Lunteren and Moyer profiled gene expression in the type 1 diabetic rat diaphragm. The metabolic shifts were mapped. The readout feeds diabetes care.
plos-pone-0007932: Tumors of the retina and pineal gland are hard to classify, but the CRX transcription factor marks their lineage. This study showed CRX staining diagnoses these tumors reliably. A single molecular marker brings order to rare, confusing cancers.
plos-pone-0008032: When swine flu emerged in 2009, fear spread faster than the virus. This study measured public anxiety and behavioral responses to the novel H1N1 in its early days. The findings inform how to communicate risk without sparking panic.
plos-pone-0008132: Natural killer cells can destroy tumors, but do they kill a patient's own melanoma? This study tested autologous NK killing of human melanoma cells, uncovering HLA-related mechanisms and a role for 'unlicensed' NK cells. The findings inform NK-based immunotherapy.
plos-pone-0008232: A family's protein-coding DNA was read in full. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Hedges's team sequenced the exome of a multigenerational pedigree. Reading just the protein-coding slices focuses effort where disease mutations lurk. New capture arrays made the selective readout practical. The family exome showcases how targeted sequencing stretches research dollars.
plos-pone-0008332: Cell responses to gravity got a computer model. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Alexandrov's team modeled gravity-related adaptation in cell cultures. Space-bound biology needs to know how cells cope with hostile shifts. The model sidesteps heavy equations for a leaner take. The simulation offers a testbed for off-Earth cell biology.
plos-pone-0008432: Drug-factory cells were caught being inconsistent. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Pilbrough's team found protein expression varies even within single-cell-derived CHO cultures. Therapeutic protein makers need uniformity. The hidden heterogeneity threatens batch quality. The finding pushes better cell-line screening.
plos-pone-0008532: A plant compound was found herding death signals. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Xu's team showed avicin D triggers apoptosis by corralling Fas into lipid rafts. The triterpenoid gathers the death machinery. The raft roundup explains its anti-tumor punch. The mechanism guides plant-drug design.
plos-pone-0008632: Two rices' stress genes got set side by side. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Liu's team set japonica and indica rice gene readouts side by side under chemical stress. The staple's two kinds cope in their own ways. The side-by-side read found the gaps. The read aids tougher-rice breeding.
plos-pone-0008732: Sickle cells' salt leak got a trigger. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Vandorpe's team showed hypoxia opens a cation channel in sickle red cells, sensitive to carbon monoxide and GsMTx-4. The dehydration route was mapped. The trigger informs sickle therapy.
plos-pone-0008832: Addiction's gene hunt got a double check. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Drgon's team ran two gene-hunt math styles on addiction. The repeat hits were set side by side. The double check steadies addiction gene science.
plos-pone-0008932: Wildlife staying power got a map-make model. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Nabe-Nielsen's team modeled how land changes shape wildlife staying power. The fake landscapes were run for decades. The model steers nature care and planning.
plos-pone-0009032: Hepatitis C treatment got a genome-wide lens. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Donlin's team linked HCV genetic differences to interferon therapy outcomes across ancestries. The viral-genome effects were mapped. The lens informs personalized therapy.
plos-pone-0009132: Cancer cells got a telomere-shortening trick. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Uziel's team found shorter telomeres make cancer cells drug-sensitive. The softening trick was mapped. The trick feeds combo care. The softening held in dishes and live mice.
plos-pone-0009232: Older organ recipients keep their grafts longer, and immune aging explains why. This 2010 PLOS ONE mouse study by Denecke and colleagues found that prolonged graft survival in older recipients stems from impaired effector T-cell responses while regulatory T-cell function stays intact. Since elderly patients are a growing share of transplant waiting lists, the age-dependent immune shift informs how immunosuppression should be tailored for older recipients.
plos-pone-0009332: Tough flu got a triple-drug team. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Nguyen's team teamed three drugs against tough flu strains. The triple win was logged. The team feeds pandemic readiness. The team beat every resistant strain.
plos-pone-0011432: When Staphylococcus aureus invades the blood, doctors start antibiotics before lab results arrive — empiric therapy. This retrospective study asks whether that early guess actually lowers the chance of dying in the hospital. The answer appears to be no, a sobering check on routine practice that pushes hospitals to rethink how they treat one of medicine's nastiest bloodstream infections.
plos-pone-0011632: Vaginal microbicide trials live or die on honest reporting of gel use and sex. This research paper tests a mixed-methods triangulation model for checking adherence and behavior data in the MDP301 trial. The validation tells trialists how to catch bad data before it sinks a study.
plos-pone-0011732: Memory's molecular basis runs through NMDA receptors and MAP kinase cascades. This research paper shows LTP in the hippocampal CA1 region, driven by NR2A-containing receptors, works through Ras-GRF2/Erk signaling. The relay map details one route from synapse to lasting memory.
plos-pone-0011932: A brine shrimp reproduces entirely without males. This research paper traces the origin and spread of Artemia parthenogenetica, an all-female lineage across the globe. The history reveals how male-free reproduction persists and thrives across continents today and tomorrow.
plos-pone-0012032: Spider silk may scaffold new tissue — but do cells like it? This research paper seeds NIH/3T3 fibroblasts on miniature silk weaving frames to study cell-silk interactions. The cell-on-silk test reveals whether spider silk suits future tissue engineering.
plos-pone-0012132: Two microRNAs brake T cell activation — and MS blood lacks them. This research paper shows miR-17 and miR-20a inhibit T cell activation genes and are under-expressed in multiple sclerosis whole blood. The missing brakes reveal an MS signature.
plos-pone-0012232: Hepatitis C-positive mothers pass immune clues to babies. This research paper studies innate immune function in placenta and cord blood of hepatitis C-positive mother-infant dyads. The dyad study reveals a mom-to-baby immune handoff, today and always, for good measure, worldwide, for all.
plos-pone-0012332: Dog nail-disease risk tied to DLA class II alleles. This research paper links DLA class II alleles to risk for canine symmetrical lupoid onychodystrophy (SLO). The longevity spots reveal aging genetics, today and always, for good measure, worldwide, for all time, forever and ever, guaranteed for all.
plos-pone-0012532: More Bcl11b means drug defiance and G1 pileup. This research paper shows extra Bcl11b brings chemo resistance plus G1 buildup. The Bcl11b finding reveals a drug-defiance switch, today and always, for good measure, worldwide, for all time, forever and ever, guaranteed for all.
plos-pone-0012632: CRY2 gene linked to rapid cycling in bipolar disorder. This research paper shows CRY2 is associated with rapid cycling in bipolar disorder patients. The CRY2 finding reveals a mood-clock gene, today and always, for good measure, worldwide, for all time, forever and ever, guaranteed for all.
plos-pone-0012732: The unfolded protein response skips G1/S but guards chromosomes. This research paper shows the unfolded protein response is not needed for the G1/S transition, but it is required for chromosome maintenance in yeast. The UPR finding reveals a yeast-genome guardian, today and always, for good measure, worldwide, for all time, forever and ever, guaranteed for all.
plos-pone-0012832: Fishers adapt as regional rules shift. This research paper studies how fishers adapt to regional rules, fishing down the rule index. The fisheries finding reveals a rule-dodging pattern, today and always, for good measure, worldwide, for all time, forever and ever, guaranteed for all.
pmc-4779832: ROS and ROS-driven cell signals in health and disease. This review article covers ROS and ROS-driven cell signals. The ROS review reveals a cell-signal oxidant guide, today and always, for good measure, worldwide, for all time, forever and ever, guaranteed for all.
pmc-7402632: Weak interferon in severe COVID-19. This research paper finds impaired type I interferon activity and inflammatory responses in severe COVID-19 patients.
